title: Identification of the untranslated sequence elements and virus-host interactions that modulate flavivirus host-specificity
text: This project will identify the precise genomic determinants and molecular mechanisms that condition the differential host ranges of insect-specific and mosquito/vertebrate flaviviruses, providing information that will assist in the rationale design of novel intervention strategies to control flavivirus transmission and disease.

title: Advancing Craniosynostosis Treatment (ACT)Rare Diseases Consortium
text:
OVERALL
The ACT Craniosynostosis Treatment (ACT) Rare Diseases Consortium aims to advance care of the 5 rare
disease types of craniosynostosis (CS) syndromes: Apert, Pfeiffer, Crouzon, Muenke, and Saethre-Chotzen.
ACT is a patient-focused, clinical research consortium of multi-disciplinary experts from 4 leading craniofacial
care centers. ACT will advance rare disease study of syndromic CS through synthesis of activities of its
Administrative, Career Enhancement, Pilot/Feasibility Cores and completion of Clinical Projects 1 and 2.

title: Predicting ECMO NeuroLogICal Injuries using mAchiNe Learning (PELICAN)
text:
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a technology to support the failing heart or lungs, allowing
time for the injured organ to heal or bridge the patient to transplant; major neurological injury is seen in more
than 1/3 of survivors, leading to long-term neurological deficits. The resulting financial costs and reduction in
quality-of-life places enormous burdens on patients, their families, and society: the ability to identify risks and
initiate a process to mitigate them would be a major advancement in the field. The proposed research will use
advanced machine learning algorithms to build a predictive model that will be refined and validated with ongoing
input from clinicians, identify modifiable risk factors for future studies, and thereby enable strategies to decrease
long-term morbidity and mortality from neurological injury.

title: A multicity study of wintertime inversions and acute cardiorespiratory health events in the western U.S.
text:
Many western U.S. cities have poor air quality during colder months; we will improve existing air quality models to
better identify the origin of these pollutants. We will estimate associations between these pollutants and acute
cardiorespiratory health events in 12 cities. We aim to inform public health interventions, develop new methods for air
quality modeling, and better understand the heath impacts of air pollution during colder months in the western U.S.

title: M-ISIC: A Multimodal Open-Source International Skin Imaging Collaboration Informatics Platform for Automated Skin Cancer Detection
text:
The proposed project targets reduction in mortality and morbidity from skin cancer via advancement of
improved informatics tools to improve artificial intelligence development and clinical education for skin
detection. Multi-modal International Skin Imaging Collaboration (M-ISIC) archive will advance machine learning
and computer vision informatics tools to support large-scale multimodal ingestion, organization, registration,
and curation of skin images and metadata datasets to improve skin cancer detection. With its open-source
tools for automatic data quality control, ingestion, organization and curation, the M-ISIC archive will support the
education of medical professionals and the development and clinical testing of automated diagnostic systems
and eventually supporting flexible clinical translation of AI algorithms.

title: Cancer Basic Biology
text: The Cancer Basic Biology (CBB) Program aims to develop fundamental new insights into the biological basis of human cancer, and to apply these insights by developing new tools and approaches to improve cancer diagnosis, therapy, and prevention. The CBB Program is the fundamental biology program of the Consortium. Our ultimate purpose is to stimulate interdisciplinary, cancer-relevant, fundamental research and develop technologies to advance capabilities in precision medicine diagnostics and therapy. Our strong record of discovery in structural, molecular, cellular, developmental, and systems biology provides mechanistic underpinning for translational cancer research across the Consortium. Our technological innovations provide the tools to understand the genetic, epigenetic, and functional changes underlying cancer and to develop creative diagnostics and therapeutics for precision medicine. To build on our legacy, we have three specific aims to 1) define fundamental mechanisms that drive normal and cancer biology, 2) understand epigenomic and genomic control of normal and cancer phenotypes, and 3) develop new tools to accelerate cancer biology research. The program’s 123 members are distributed over all three Consortium institutions, providing integration across the Consortium. Our research spans the spectrum from hypothesis-driven, mechanistic analysis, through to the detection and description of cancer-induced changes in the genome, epigenome, transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome, as well as the rational design of molecules and experimental workflows to manipulate cells and understand the molecular and cellular basis of cancer. Insights from these fundamental discoveries advance development of new cancer diagnostics and therapeutics. Program members currently have $37.4M in research funding, of which $7.6M is from NCI and $14.5M is from NIH. During this cycle, members published 836 cancer-relevant papers, of which 16% were intraprogrammatic and 22% were interprogrammatic. To promote collaborative science, the program leadership also spans the three Consortium institutions with expertise in basic and translational cancer biology. Our members are active in training and mentoring, including holding leadership positions in prebaccalaureate and predoctoral training programs, and connect with underserved populations in the catchment area through pilot projects and outreach programs. Program leadership works with Consortium Shared Resources to ensure support for state-of-the-art investigation. Program trainees participate in pan- institutional events and symposia designed to expose basic scientists to cancer problems and encourage them to apply their skills to collaborative projects.

title: Molecular Basis of Viral Infectivity
text:
The goal of this training grant is to provide students who 1) are well trained in the study of mechanisms of viral
replication, 2) can investigate human viruses causing disease, such as the human immunodeficiency virus and
herpes viruses, 3) can investigate new antiviral compounds and vaccines to prevent or treat viral diseases, 4)
can study viruses that are emerging threats to human health, and 5) can use viruses to probe the cellular and
molecular biology of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

title: The multifaceted pathways of astrovirus entry and egress
text:
Astroviruses are a major cause of pediatric diarrhea worldwide, but we lack a clear understanding of how they
replicate inside of cells. Small intestinal goblet cells, specialized epithelial cells that produce mucus, are
targeted by astrovirus as well as other respiratory and enteric viruses for infection. The purpose of this work is
to define the entry and exit steps of the astrovirus replication cycle using novel goblet cell models so that we
can build the foundation for future treatment and prevention strategies.

title: Handheld and population-based sequencing for rapid detection of new and repurposed drug resistance in M. tuberculosis
text:
Our overall goal is to improve patient outcomes through development and evaluation of novel sequencing
strategies in order to facilitate early, appropriate drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment under programmatic
conditions, and to preserve new shorter course treatment regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis.

title: Mechanisms of SOX2 Regulation in Glioblastoma
text:
Despite progress in surgery and chemoradiation therapies, the prognosis of the brain cancer glioblastoma
remains challenging; in addition to the blood-brain barrier, treatment resistance in glioblastoma has been
attributed to the intrinsic heterogeneity of these tumors. One specific glioblastoma cell type, the glioblastoma
stem cell, has been the focus of intense investigation because these cancer cells can resist therapy and therefore
drive tumor recurrence after treatment. Here we propose to examine the molecular regulation of the SOX2
transcription factor, which is critical for the malignant behavior of glioblastoma stem cells, with our long-term goal
being to leverage SOX2-dependent mechanisms to halt tumor growth and overcome therapy resistance in
patients.

title: Pathogenesis of Airway Stem Cell Abnormalities in Obliterative Bronchiolitis
text:
Project Narrative/Public Health Relevance:
Lung transplantation is an effective treatment for end-stage lung disease, which is predicted to be the third
leading cause of death worldwide by 2030; however, survival is limited by the development of chronic lung
allograft dysfunction (CLAD) in the transplanted lungs. The objective of this proposal is to determine the
mechanisms by which airway stem cells such as submucosal gland-derived myoepithelial cells and basal stem
cell are altered in allografts and contribute to the pathogenesis of CLAD. This is expected to identify markers to
enable early diagnosis of CLAD and uncover novel therapeutic options for this condition.

title: MDSRC for Next Directions in Muscular Dystrophy Research
text:
The Research Institute at Nationwide Children’s Hospital proposes a Muscular Dystrophy
Specialized Research Center that builds upon our extensive expertise in therapeutic
development, including first-in-human gene therapies, with a Shared Resource Core that
develops critical patient-derived reagents for testing of new therapies, a Training Core that
builds upon our nationally-recognized myology training program, and Projects intended to
develop the next generation of therapies beyond microdystrophin gene therapy.

title: Regulation of adult hippocampal function by the neural stem and progenitor cell secretome
text:
The persistence of neural stem cells in isolated niches of the adult brain offers a potentially unique source of
plasticity and regeneration. Understanding how neural stem cells contribute to adult brain plasticity is critical to
determining the health-relevance of these cell populations. The proposed experiments will dissect the functional
role of neural stem cell secreted proteins in modulating the physiology and behavioral function of the adult
hippocampus, a brain region which mediates essential memory and affect functions which are impaired in
numerous brain diseases and injuries.

title: Perfecting tools to define the glycan-protein interactome
text:
Glycans, sugar structures carried on glycoproteins and glycolipids, are abundant on cell surfaces where they
regulate cell health via interaction with glycan-specific binding proteins. Deciphering the “glycan code” of cell
regulation is a key goal for glycobiology that has great potential to impact human health in clinical areas
including cancer diagnosis and therapy, immune system disorders, and nervous system diseases. This
focused Technology Research and Development application combines the power of chemistry and deep
learning computation to the identification and structural determination of glycan-protein interactions.

title: Towards Safe and Efficacious Medical Therapy for Patients with Clinically Non-Functioning Pituitary Tumors
text:
Clinically non-functioning pituitary tumors (CNFTs) account for one-third of all pituitary adenomas. Surgical
resection is the current standard of care for CNFTs but complete resection is infrequently achieved due to their
size and invariable invasion of locally adjacent structures. In this highly innovative project, we will combine a
unique patient-derived 3D tumoroid human CNFT model which recapitulates the pituitary tumor cell molecular
phenotype with an automated high throughput screen to identify novel tumoricidal and growth inhibitory
compounds.

title: Novel Assessments of the Health Impacts of Tropical Cyclones
text: In the United States, tropical cyclones, such as hurricanes and tropical storms, have a devastating effect on society, yet a comprehensive assessment of their health impacts is still lacking. The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on quantifying the hospitalization and mortality burden of tropical cyclones while also characterizing physical factors that drive differences in impacts on communities. The results of this project are expected to greatly benefit understanding of the health impacts of tropical cyclone exposure and create actionable results.

title: Metabolic regulation of muscle satellite cell homeostasis
text:
Skeletal muscle satellite cells (MuSCs) are tissue stem cells responsible for muscle repair in response to injury
and degenerative diseases. This project aims to investigate the novel role played by lipid droplets and lipid
metabolism in satellite cell biology. Knowledge from the proposed work will lead to better understanding of the
cellular and molecular regulation of MuSC function in the context of muscle regeneration under pathological
conditions.

title: New approach methodologies using stem cell morphogenesis models for preclinical developmental toxicity screening
text:
Proposal Narrative
 The proposed study is to establish validated New Approach Methodologies, or NAMs, for the
assessment of developmental toxicity using the morphogenesis models of pluripotent stem cells. The
overarching goal is to apply such NAMs to reduce and replace live animal toxicity tests, the latter of which are
increasingly scrutinized for being time-consuming, costly, and ethically challenging.

title: Structural Basis of Programmable DNA-Insertion via Cryo-EM Studies of CRISPR-Associated TnsC
text:
CRISPR-transposase systems show tremendous potential to be generally useful programmable DNA-
insertion tools to complement the power of CRISPR-Cas9, however the mechanisms governing DNA-insertion
are mysterious and subject to unknown regulatory ‘rules’ that inhibit wide-spread adoption. We propose to
characterize the mechanisms that govern programmed DNA-insertion using high-resolution cryo-EM focusing
on the regulatory component, TnsC, from the shCAST system. Our structures will provide a detailed
understanding of how CRISPR-transposase systems function at the molecular level; this information will enable
engineering of the shCAST system to become a generally useful genome-editing tool.

title: Establishing human stem cell derived-retinal organoids as functional models of human retina for studying disease and testing therapies
text:
A major cause of blindness is degeneration of photoreceptors in the retina and there is no available cure or
therapy that can restore sight in such cases. Human stem cell derived retinal tissue (Retinal Organoid or RO)
hold tremendous promise as a robust model system for replicating diseases and testing therapeutics but suffer
from as yet undetermined limitations that prevent homogenous functional profiles and connectivity between the
constituent retinal neurons. Our proposed research will determine these limitations within ROs to ultimately
improve RO functionality and authenticity, and also determine the value of ROs as a reliable platform to model
diseases and test the efficacy of gene therapy for functional restoration.
